newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chronology of Nomura Securities scandal.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Nomura Securities scandal.

text.p: Following is a brief chronology of the payoff scandal involving Nomura Securities Co Ltd, which led on Tuesday to Japan's securities watchdog recommending administrative penalties against the firm.

March 6, 1997 -- Nomura announces that an internal probe found two of its directors had been involved in what appear to be illegal deals: the transfer of money from a Nomura account to a corporate client's account.

March 10, 1997 -- Nomura directors Shimpei Matsuki and Nobutaka Fujikura resign after internal probes found they made discretionary deals banned under Japanese securities exchange law and funnelled profits to a company affiliated with a racketeer.

March 14, 1997 -- Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki steps down to became an adviser to the company to atone for a scandal over suspected illegal deals. Chairman Masashi Suzuki takes on the job of president in addition to the chairmanship.
March 25, 1997 -- Tokyo prosecutors start investigating a Nomura director's payment of 38 million yen to a company run by a relative of a racketeer to avoid disruption of a Nomura annual meeting.
April 18, 1997 -- A former president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd 8604.t, Hideo Sakamaki, answers questions at a finance committee meeting of Japan's Lower House of parliament.
May 14, 1997 -- Tokyo prosecutors arrest three former Nomura officials.
May 15, 1997 -- Tokyo prosecutors arrest racketeer Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother.

May 30, 1997 -- Tokyo prosecutors arrest Nomura's Sakamaki on suspicion of violating the Commercial Code and the Securities and Exchange Law by conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen to Ryuichi Koike in 1995.

June 4, 1997 -- Prosecutors indict Nomura itself and two of its former executives. Nomura is indicted on charges of violating the Securities and Exchange Law and two former executives are indicted on charges of violating the Securities and Exchange Law and the Commercial Code by paying 49.7 million yen to Ryuichi Koike between January and June 1995 in exchange for not disrupting the Nomura shareholders' general meeting in June, 1995.

June 19, 1997 -- Prosecutors indict former Nomura president Sakamaki on charges of making illegal payoffs to a racketeer. The indictment alleges that Sakamaki paid 49.73 million yen to Koike between January 31 and June 15, 1995.
July 8, 1997 -- Japanese media report that Nomura is suspected of making illegal payoffs to two racketeers other than Ryuichi Koike.
Although the payments violate Japan's Commercial Code, the two racketeers could escape prosecution because a three-year statute of limitations has run out, the reports say.

July 9, 1997 -- Tokyo prosecutors indict for a second time former president Hideo Sakamaki and former managing director Nobutaka Fujikura. The two are charged with conspiring with other Nomura officials to pay 320 million yen in cash to racketeer Ryuichi Koike around March 24, 1995.

July 15, 1997 -- Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), recommends to the Ministry of Finance that it assess penalties against Nomura for violating the Securities and Exchange Law. The SESC says Nomura was at fault for inadequate internal controls.
